overview.text: Asian cultivated rice, Oryza sativa, is an annual, semi-aquatic grass grown for its edible grain. A major staple crop worldwide, it has been adapted to very different farming landscapes. Rice can grow in deeply flooded fields as well as dry, hilly uplands, so paddies are common but not essential. Two familiar groups are indica, often associated with long, non-sticky grains and tropical lowlands, and japonica, often associated with shorter, sticky grains and temperate or upland settings. Over millennia, communities have reshaped hillsides and directed water to cultivate rice, linking this crop to distinctive agricultural landscapes and food traditions.

key_facts.text: Asian rice is Oryza sativa, an annual, semi-aquatic grass. African rice, Oryza glaberrima, is a separate domesticated species.
Rice is a major staple food crop worldwide; the USDA describes it as a staple for more than half the world’s population.
Rice grows in diverse conditions, from deeply flooded fields to dry, hilly uplands; flooding is common in cultivation but not essential.
Indica rice is commonly associated with long, non-sticky grains and tropical lowlands; japonica is associated with stickier grains and temperate or upland settings.
Rice cultivation has involved reshaping steep hillsides into terraces and building systems to channel water into fields.
